title: Carbon and Macromolecules
seo_title: Macromolecules Worksheets: Carbohydrates, Lipids, Proteins and Nucleic Acids (Biology)
standard_text: Construct and revise an explanation based on evidence for how carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen from sugar molecules may combine with other elements to form amino acids and/or other large carbon-based molecules.
meta_desc: Free high school biology worksheets on macromolecules (NGSS HS-LS1-6): carbohydrates, lipids, proteins and nucleic acids, monomers, elements and dehydration synthesis. 100 questions with answers.
key_sub: C, H and O from sugar, plus N and P, build proteins, fats and nucleic acids.
body_html:
How to think about it

Small units join into big molecules. Sugars made in photosynthesis supply C, H and O; adding N (and P, S) makes the other molecules.

MacromoleculeMonomerElements
carbohydratesmonosaccharides (simple sugars like glucose)C, H and O
proteinsamino acidsC, H, O and N (some also S)
lipidsfatty acids and glycerolC, H and O
nucleic acidsnucleotidesC, H, O, N and P
Example

10 amino acids join. Water released?

One water per bond

10 − 1

Answer: 9

Example

Glycine is C2H5NO2. How many atoms?

2 + 5 + 1 + 2

Answer: 10

Common mistakes

  • Thinking fats are made of amino acids. They are made of fatty acids and glycerol.
  • Thinking proteins have only C, H and O. They also have N.
  • Counting n water molecules for n monomers. It is n − 1.

faq.q: How do sugars become amino acids?
faq.a: Cells rearrange the C, H and O from sugars and add nitrogen (and sometimes sulfur) to build amino acids.
Joining two monomers by removing a water molecule. A chain of n monomers releases n − 1 waters.
